name: Dimensional weight
seoTitle: Dimensional weight Calculator: Free, With Steps
seoDesc: Dimensional weight: work out dimensional weight (FedEx) from the length and the width. A free other calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Dimensional weight calculator turns the length and the width into dimensional weight (FedEx). That makes it useful for whatever you happen to be working on. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Dimensional weight calculator work?
sections.html:
The Dimensional weight calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports dimensional weight (FedEx) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the units and the rate); then you type in the length (Measurements), the length (Measurements), the width (Measurements) and the width (Measurements).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

sections.title: The formula behind the Dimensional weight calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Dimensional weight=rounded up, ((1 ÷ 139) × height × length × width)
Dimensional weight=rounded up, ((1 ÷ 166) × height × length × width)
Dimensional weight=rounded up, ((1 ÷ 5000) × height × length × width)
Dimensional weight=rounded up, (height × length × width ÷ rate)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Units set to cm/kg, Length = 30 in, Width = 30 in and Height = 30 in. Working through the relationship above gives Dimensional weight = 1 lb.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Dimensional weight = 1 lb should be roughly the size you expected from Units set to cm/kg and Length = 30 in.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Dimensional weight calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the length and the width — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?

  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the Dimensional weight calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns dimensional weight (FedEx), derived from the length and the width. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Dimensional weight calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the length and the width, which is 10 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter length (Measurements) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Length (Measurements) opens in inches and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Dimensional weight = 1 lb. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Dimensional weight calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
